verses.translation_literal: A song of the ascents, of David. YHWH, not has been lofty my heart, and not have been lifted up my eyes, and not have I walked in great things and in things too wonderful for me.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song for the climbing road, David's own. LORD, my heart has not swelled with pride. My eyes have not gone up to look down on others. I have not gone wandering after things too vast, too marvelous for me to hold.
verses.directors_commentary: Play this as a quiet, almost surprised confession, not a boast. The pilgrim songs (the 'ascents') were sung on the road up to Jerusalem, so the first audience is walking uphill while it hears a man say he has no wish to climb higher than his place. The Hebrew builds its denial in three layers: heart (the inner wish), eyes (the visible look, the raised gaze of the arrogant) and feet (the way a person walks through life). Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David both read heart and eyes as the hidden and the open sides of pride. The key word is 'walked': the Hebrew says halakh, 'I have gone about', with the sense of a life-course, and the KJV's 'exercise myself in great matters' turns a road image into a gymnasium. The KJV also reads 'wonderful' as 'high', which flattens niflaʾot, the word used elsewhere for God's own marvels: the man is saying that wonders belong to God and not to him. Rashi reads 'great things' as grand building and planting, and Metzudat David too as palaces and towers, which makes this a king renouncing display. Radak reads it as intellect: not forcing into divine mysteries. Both are possible, so keep the line open and let the actor decide which weight to carry.

philological_notes.note: To be high, and so haughty. Said of the heart, it means pride, not height. The verb is perfect, 'has not been' as a settled fact of character, not a single act.

'I have walked'; the doubled lamed has the look of an intensive stem, yet Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as intransitive, 'I have gone about in', which supports 'walked in' over the KJV's 'exercise myself in'.
Things too wonderful or difficult; the same root names God's marvellous acts. The point is that such things are beyond the speaker's reach ('from me'), not forbidden.

verses.translation_literal: If not I have levelled and I have silenced my soul, like a weaned [child] upon his mother, like the weaned [child] upon me my soul.
verses.translation_dramatic: No. I have stilled my soul. I have hushed it, the way a weaned child lies quiet against its mother. Like that child, calm and unclamoring, so my soul rests within me.
verses.directors_commentary:
Begin with the first two words. 'Im lo', literally 'if not', is the stub of an oath: 'if I have not done this, may such and such befall me'. The punishment is left unsaid, as Radak and Metzudat David both note, and Meiri compares the unfinished oath of the spies in Numbers. Played as a bare 'if not', it sounds like a man swearing so hard he forgets to finish. The KJV's 'Surely' catches the force but hides the oath; the ASV has the same flat assertion.

Then the two verbs, which the KJV turns into 'behaved and quieted'. The first, shiviti, is 'I have made level, set even', the image of a rough surface smoothed, a swelling pride pressed flat, and a fine answer to verse 1's 'my heart has not swelled'. The second, vedomamti, is 'I have made silent', from the root of stillness. The doubling continues: the verse says its simile twice. Ibn Ezra says the sense is simply doubled, and Metzudat David says the repetition expresses persistence, a vow kept again and again. Malbim hears something sharper and divides the work: the first verb goes with 'like a weaned child upon his mother', meaning that I have put all my trust in the LORD alone, as the child puts his on his mother; the second goes with 'like a weaned child upon me', meaning that my soul is silent like the weaned child, who has no word to say without his mother, and who knows that in itself it has no strength. The mother it leans on is God, as verse 3 makes plain. Tell your actor which reading they play; the line works as insistence or as two images.

The weaned child is not the nursing baby. Gamul is a child past the breast, at about two or three years, as with Isaac in Genesis 21:8, a child old enough to be loud for milk and now taught not to. The BBE's 'child on its mother's breast' reverses this: the whole point is that the child no longer demands the breast and is calm in her arms anyway. Radak reads the child who still leans on his mother as the mind that relies on teachers and received tradition, and Metzudat David as trust in the LORD. The last word order is also tight and odd: 'like the weaned child upon me, my soul', with the noun held back to land last. The KJV's 'even as a weaned child' smooths that over, and 'upon me' is hard to render. Rashi takes it as 'within my inner part'.

philological_notes.note: The beginning of an oath formula, with the curse left unspoken ('if I have not ..., may ...'). The commentators agree on this and Meiri parallels the spies passage in Numbers. English has no neat equivalent, so the literal layer keeps 'if not'.

From shavah, 'to be level, even', here in the intensive stem, so 'I have levelled, set even'. The image is the smoothing of something swollen, the opposite of verse 1's pride. Ibn Ezra glosses it as 'I have set', and Metzudat Zion derives it from shaveh.

A passive participle, 'one who has been weaned', the child just moved away from the mother's breast. The same root is used of Isaac in Genesis 21:8. The image is of a child that is quiet while nursing is over, and not of a baby still at the breast.

verses.translation_literal: Wait, Israel, for YHWH, from now and until forever.
verses.translation_dramatic: Israel, wait for the LORD. Wait now, and go on waiting, for as long as time will run.
verses.directors_commentary: The voice widens at once from one quiet soul to a whole crowd on the road. This is an imperative, as Ibn Ezra says, and not a wish: the KJV's 'Let Israel hope' softens a command into a polite permission. The verb yachal means to wait with strained expectation, almost to stretch toward something, so the English 'hope' is weaker than the Hebrew; it is the waiting of the weaned child who stays near its mother, now turned on God. Metzudat David hears David saying 'look at me, and do as I did', and Malbim hears God as the mother Israel never outgrows, since Israel, unlike a child, never leaves her. 'From now and until forever' is a pair of time markers that stretch the stillness of verse 2 into the whole span of the pilgrim's life. For the first audience, climbing toward the Temple, 'now' is the very step they are taking.

philological_notes.note: Imperative 'wait, hope', a taut expectant waiting. Ibn Ezra stresses it is a command.
'From now and until forever', a fixed formula of the Psalms covering all time from the present.
